covalent.note: Covalent radius; PubChem's values are those of Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832.

vdw.note: Van der Waals radius (Los Alamos National Laboratory).

allen.note: Configuration energy (Allen electronegativity) in eV, not converted to the Pauling-like scale; Mann 2000a.

polarizability.note: Recommended value of the 2018 table: from experiment where it is precise enough, otherwise from high-level calculation.

crust.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for Earth's crust, via PubChem ('2.36×10⁴ milligrams per kilogram').

ocean.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for sea water, via PubChem ('1.08×10⁴ milligrams per liter').

solar.note: Proto-solar (4.567 Ga ago) elemental mass fraction, column 'Elemental Mass Fractions' of ESM Table A13; the table gives no uncertainty (relative sigma of N(E) in Table 6 applies).

solarLogEps.note: A(E) = log10(N_E/N_H) + 12, 'Solar System Present' log (E/H)+12; basis: average of solar and meteoritic values; unc = 1 sigma in dex as printed.

body.note: In a 70 kg reference adult (ICRP Publication 23, 1975, Table 110).

crystal.reference: Wyckoff, R. W. G. (1963). Crystal Structures 1, 7.
crystal.note: bcc at 293 K, value from Wyckoff's compilation (no primary reference in CIF). Sodium transforms to close-packed forms at low temperature (not covered here).

production.basis: mine production, salt (NaCl, gross weight, all types)

tonnesPerYear.note: World mine production, salt (NaCl, gross weight, all types), 2025 (USGS: 270,000 thousand metric tons).

origin.note: Read off Fig. 39 at the dotted 'age of the Sun' line (t = 9.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, 4.6 Gyr ago): pixel fractions of the stacked areas (agb 0.137, massive_stars 0.863); quantised to 0.05. Stack height 62 px. Paper: 'For the elements from Ne to Ge, the newly synthesized amounts are very small for AGB stars, and the small green areas are mostly for mass loss.'

air.text: Tarnishes quickly to a dull grey and burns in air when heated, forming sodium oxide.

water.text: Reacts violently with water, giving sodium hydroxide and hydrogen, which often catches fire.

acids.text: Reacts violently with acids, forming the sodium salts (with hydrochloric acid, common salt).

splitting.note: Ground-state A constant (From Arimondo, Inguscio and Violino (1977)), as tabulated by Allegrini, Arimondo and Orozco (2022); splitting = |A|(I + 1/2).

gamma.note: Γ/2π from NIST's A_ki = 6.16e+07 s⁻¹ (accuracy class AA), taking the upper level to decay only on this line; where it has other decay channels the true linewidth is slightly larger.

laserCooling.note: The 1987 paper is the first magneto-optical trap of any atom; BEC 1995, one of the two first BECs. Repumping uses the other ground hyperfine level on the same D2 line, so no separate repump wavelength is given.

plantRole.text: Essential for some C4 and CAM plants, which use it to move pyruvate into chloroplasts; can partly replace potassium as an osmoticum, and halophytes store it in large amounts.

humanRole.text: The main positive ion outside cells; controls water balance and, with potassium, nerve signals.

environment.text: Salt, mostly sodium chloride, in irrigated and naturally saline soils limits crop yields worldwide; most crops suffer when sodium builds up in their leaves.

history.nameOrigin: Named by Davy after soda (caustic soda), the compound he split by electrolysis to obtain it.
history.symbolNote: Na comes from the Latin natrium, after natron, a naturally occurring soda salt.
history.note: Obtained by electrolysis of molten caustic soda at the Royal Institution, soon after potassium.

prose.text: Sodium is a soft, silvery alkali metal that can be cut with a knife and must be kept under oil, because it reacts vigorously with water; we meet it every day in table salt and as the ions that help carry signals along our nerves. It melts at about 371 K (98 °C), below the boiling point of water. The yellow glow of salt in a flame, and of old street lamps, is a pair of lines at 589.0 and 589.6 nm. Both come from the lone 3s electron ([Ne] 3s¹) falling back from 3p, a level split in two by spin–orbit coupling into ²P°₃/₂ and ²P°₁/₂.
